cards.title: Create WooCommerce affiliate products with external/affiliate product type
cards.summary: Set up an affiliate product in WooCommerce by switching product type to external/affiliate, adding your affiliate link and price label, so you earn commission without holding inventory.
cards.use_when: Merchandising: you want to add a partner tool, brand or recommended gear to your catalog and earn affiliate commission on click-through rather than selling stocked goods.
steps: Create a new product and switch the product type dropdown to 'External/Affiliate product' in the linked product data area.
Paste your affiliate link into the product URL field and set the button text (e.g. 'More information' or 'See plans') in the button text field.
Enter the starting price (e.g. '$5 per month') and add a short description of the partner product.
Assign a relevant category (e.g. 'tools').
Fix cropped product images: open the image in an editor, expand the canvas to a square (e.g. 1000x1000 px) and re-upload so the tile displays correctly on the shop archive.
Publish and view the product; confirm the button links out through your affiliate URL.
caveats: Affiliate products do not use your checkout or inventory — the transaction happens on the partner site, so you cannot offer your own coupons or control the post-purchase experience.
If no related-product block appears, that is expected until you add upsells/cross-sells manually.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Add WooCommerce upsells (product page) vs cross-sells (cart)
cards.summary: Configure upsells to appear on a product page and cross-sells in the cart, and understand that cross-sells are only triggered by the specific product in the cart.
cards.use_when: Merchandising / AOV: you want to lift average order value by recommending complementary products at the product page or in the cart.
steps: Open the product, go to the 'Linked products' section in product data.
Add one or more products to the 'Upsells' field — these display on the product page (theme-dependent, often as 'You may also like').
Add one or more products to the 'Cross-sells' field — these display in the cart below the cart line items.
Update the product and verify by viewing the product page (upsells) and adding the product to the cart (cross-sells).
Test remove: if you empty the triggering product from the cart, the cross-sells disappear because they are tied to that specific product.
caveats: Cross-sells only show when a matching product is in the cart, so they will not surface for unrelated carts.
Upsell placement and label text depend on the active theme.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Customize shop look with fonts, spacing and archive layout
cards.summary: Use the WordPress customizer typography and WooCommerce product archive settings to control fonts, product card layout, spacing and colors, especially to lift the heavy title area above the product grid.
cards.use_when: PDP/landing page and storefront design: your product archive looks cluttered or off-brand and you want to tighten the top area and standardize typography before running traffic.
steps: Pick fonts on fonts.google.com (filter by category, e.g. sans-serif). Use one font for headings and another for body text for contrast.
In the customizer's typography settings, set the base font (e.g. Open Sans) and set the heading/title font (e.g. Nunito Sans).
Under the appearance menu, set the menu font to the heading font; adjust capitalisation, letter spacing (e.g. 0.05) and size.
On the product archive, reduce or remove the big page title area so products appear higher; toggle the display type to control whether pricing shows.
Turn on 'add to cart and price' cart options if you want those on the archive, or use a variation layout (e.g. variation type 1) with image, title, price ordering.
Drag archive element order (image, title, price, rating, taxonomies) to rearrange; set image border radius (1em ≈ 16px) and confirm a hover zoom if desired.
Match colors (price, taxonomies, buttons) to your brand palette; add custom CSS (e.g. rounded buttons) under Additional CSS and publish.
caveats: Exact settings, labels and preview behavior depend on the active theme (shown here with a free theme).
If you want a test order flow, remember to disable 'coming soon' maintenance mode first.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Sell to specific countries and set flexible table-rate shipping by price tiers
cards.summary: Restrict selling/shipping to specific countries and configure the Flexible Shipping (table-rate) plugin to charge shipping based on cart price tiers, with a free-shipping threshold.
cards.use_when: Fulfillment / pricing: you ship to a limited set of countries and want shipping cost that scales with order value instead of a flat rate.
steps: Go to WooCommerce → Settings → General, set Selling locations to 'Sell to specific countries' (or all except some) and list the target countries.
Remove the default free-shipping method in WooCommerce → Settings → Shipping → Shipping zones.
Install and activate a table-rate plugin (e.g. 'Flexible Shipping' from Octolize) from the plugin repository; keep it updated.
Add a shipping method to each zone, name the carrier (e.g. UPS), and set a free-shipping minimum order value (e.g. $200).
Build price-based rules, e.g. $0–$99.99 = $6.99, $20–$49.99 = $8.99 (adjust band edges to be non-overlapping), $50–$99.99 = $12.99, $100–$199.99 = $14.99.
If your band edges overlap, items get placed in the widest matching region — review band boundaries carefully.
Alternatively switch the rule basis to weight; set product weights/dimensions and adjust weight/length units in WooCommerce → Settings → Products.
Repeat the whole method for each additional country zone (e.g. Canada with FedEx and a different free-shipping threshold).
caveats: The example price tiers and free-shipping thresholds are the presenter's own setup, not universal rules — set your own based on margins.
Table-rate plugins and their settings screens change over time; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Configure tax rates by country, state and product class
cards.summary: Enable WooCommerce taxes, build standard/reduced/zero rate classes, assign product tax classes, and choose whether displayed prices include tax — matching the whole customer journey.
cards.use_when: Pricing/checkout: you sell physical, book/reduced and digital products across multiple countries and need tax to calculate correctly and display consistently.
steps: Ensure the store address is filled in, then enable taxes in WooCommerce → Settings → General; the Tax tab appears.
Understand the three classes: standard (normal physical products), reduced (e.g. books), zero (e.g. digital in the US). Add custom classes if needed.
In Standard rates, add per-region rows: e.g. US 20%, Canada 30% (fill in real rates for your business).
In Reduced/Zero rates, set the appropriate percentages per country.
To decide whether tax is added on shipping, turn it on if you sell to companies.
Assign a product's Tax class (standard/reduced/zero) on the product's General tab — this changes the tax applied at cart/checkout.

Choose how prices display: enter prices inclusive or exclusive of tax, and set whether prices in shop / cart / checkout display including tax. Aim for a consistent number across product page → cart → checkout.
To calculate taxes per US state, look up state rates (e.g. California 7.25%, Nevada 6.85%) and add each state row, checking the correct state code.
Alternatively use WooCommerce automated taxes (paid add-on) via the plugin search to avoid manual state-by-state entry.
caveats: The example percentages used in the tutorial are illustrative, not real tax advice — apply your own jurisdiction's rules.
Display price inclusive vs exclusive changes the cart line maths; mixing shop-inclusive with checkout-exclusive causes confusing prices.
Automated tax is a paid tool; whether it is worth it depends on your volume.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Generate legal pages content and add them to the footer menu
cards.summary: Draft the legal pages you need (privacy, terms, returns, etc.) with an AI assistant and publish them into a footer legal menu so they are linked from every page.
cards.use_when: Store setup: you are preparing to launch and need compliant legal pages without paying for legal drafting, and want them discoverable sitewide.
steps: Ask an AI assistant: 'I sell [category] in [countries]. Which legal pages do I need? Create the content, and tell me what info you need from my company.'
Provide your legal company name, business address and product category so the drafts are specific.
In the customizer's menus, create a new menu (e.g. 'Legal') and add pages: Privacy Policy, Terms and Conditions, and any additional required policies.
Paste the generated content into each page and publish.
Edit the footer, remove any placeholder info, and add the Legal menu so it appears sitewide.
Save and preview each legal page from the live site to confirm content and links render.
caveats: AI-drafted legal text is a starting point, not legal advice — have it reviewed for your jurisdiction and business model.
Requirements differ by country and product type (e.g. subscription, digital, furniture), so verify what applies to you.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Enable card, PayPal and wallet payments (Stripe + PayPal) and test the flow
cards.summary: Install the WooCommerce Stripe gateway to accept cards and wallets, add PayPal as a secondary method, run a test-mode order, then flip to live and simplify the checkout fields.
cards.use_when: Checkout: you are launching a store and need working card, PayPal and wallet payment methods before sending real traffic.
steps: Install 'WooCommerce Stripe Payment Gateway' from the plugin directory and click activate.
Connect your Stripe account via the on-screen flow (returning redirects to WooCommerce).
In Stripe settings, enable test mode first; create/connect a test account to generate the webhook so payouts and webhook status show enabled.
Optionally turn on Apple Pay / Google Pay in the payment settings and hide them on product pages if you don't want express buttons there.
Install 'WooCommerce PayPal Payments' and connect your business PayPal account; enable it and set your preferred payment method order (drag card above PayPal, or vice versa).
Place a test order to confirm the buyer confirmation email and the seller new-order email both fire.
When ready, uncheck test mode on Stripe so live payments are enabled, then place a live test order.

In the customizer's WooCommerce → Checkout page settings, hide unnecessary fields (company name, second address line) and make phone optional if you don't need it, then link the Privacy Policy and Terms pages so buyers must agree before ordering.
caveats: Live mode uses real cards and real charges — verify amounts before finalising.
Plugin settings, webhook naming and account-connection steps change over time; confirm the current interface before following screenshots.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Handle incoming orders and manage WooCommerce order statuses
cards.summary: Use order statuses to move an order from Processing to Completed when physical goods ship, or to Cancelled/Refunded as needed, which triggers the appropriate customer emails.
cards.use_when: Fulfillment: you have live orders and need a repeatable process for processing, shipping, completing or refunding them.
steps: Go to WooCommerce → Orders and open an order.
For paid physical orders the status starts as Processing (the buyer receives 'we received your order and it's now being processed').
After shipping, change the status to Completed and update — the buyer then receives the completed-order email (e.g. 'good things are heading your way').
Use Cancelled or Refunded statuses when the order doesn't proceed.

Because products, shipping, taxes and payments are already configured, the only manual step for physical goods is dispatching the shipment — digital products and services need no manual shipping step.
caveats: Status-to-email mapping depends on your WooCommerce email settings; verify which emails are sent to customer vs admin.
Automated flows cover the order lifecycle but physical fulfilment still requires you (or your 3PL) to ship.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Brand transactional order emails (colors, logo, copy)
cards.summary: Style and edit WooCommerce customer emails — colors, logo, headings and body copy — so transactional messages match the store's branding and read clearly.
cards.use_when: Retention / post-purchase: your order confirmation emails look generic and you want them consistent with your brand and better worded.
steps: Go to WooCommerce → Settings → Emails to see the list of customer and admin emails; each shows a preview of the email it corresponds to.
Copy the site's primary color from the customizer's colors section and paste it into the email style color field so the buttons/accents match.
Upload your logo, set the logo size (e.g. 120) and alignment, and confirm site title / store address text lower in the email.
Edit the processing email's heading (e.g. 'your order at [store].com has been received') and additional content (e.g. a help/contact line).

To change hard-coded template strings, copy the WooCommerce email template file to the theme (Appearance → Theme File Editor → WooCommerce → emails) and edit the PHP text, or copy the template into your child theme first.
Set the From name (e.g. 'Ferdy from SofaSupa') and From address so replies route correctly, then send a test email or place a test order.
caveats: Editing theme PHP directly means theme updates can overwrite your changes — the tutorial explicitly notes making a copy; use a child theme in practice.
Changing wording in the settings only covers the fields exposed there; deeper copy lives in template files.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Connect OmniSend to WooCommerce and brand the account
cards.summary: Install the OmniSend plugin to sync a WooCommerce store with an email platform so you can build lists, send campaigns and track email-attributed revenue.
cards.use_when: Retention/acquisition: you want an email list and marketing automation tied to your store, plus revenue attribution from email.
steps: Sign up at OmniSend via email (business email), verify via the link sent to that inbox.
Enter store details (name, URL), platform (WooCommerce) and current provider (or 'none'), business address and time zone.
Install the OmniSend plugin from the plugin uploader (download the connect plugin, then upload → install → activate).
Click 'connect your store' and approve the required permissions; OmniSend will attempt to grab your branding colors automatically.
Set brand assets: accent/dark/light colors from the customizer, upload a logo PNG, choose heading fonts, add social links if wanted, then save brand assets.
Note whether you migrated from another provider — OmniSend offers a migration service via a form (claimed completion within five business days).
Track email-attributed revenue in the OmniSend dashboard once sending begins.
caveats: The free tier has a monthly sending cap (500 emails/month shown) and displays OmniSend branding; paid tiers remove branding and raise limits.
Automated migration timing is the vendor's claim, not a guarantee.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Build a discount opt-in pop-up to grow the email list
cards.summary: Create an OmniSend opt-in form that offers a first-order discount in exchange for name and email, control when it triggers, and match it to the store's styling.
cards.use_when: Acquisition/retention: you want to capture emails on-site by offering a discount pop-up instead of relying only on paid traffic.
steps: In OmniSend, go to Forms and pick a template (e.g. a simple pop-up offering 'get 10% off your first order').
Edit the heading and copy, then add a first-name field and remove its label so it reads 'enter your first name'.
Match the store style: set button corner radius, field radius, fonts and colors to the site's existing look, and make the success message in capital letters/style consistent.

Set display rules: trigger after a time on site (e.g. 3–10 seconds), after scrolling a percentage (e.g. 30%) or on exit intent; set the frequency so it reappears e.g. once per day after being dismissed.
Choose display type (pop-up, flyout, landing page or embed) and device targeting.
Enable the form so it goes live on the store — the connected store means enabling it triggers the pop-up on-site.
Optionally include a phone field only if you plan to send SMS, otherwise remove it to reduce friction.
caveats: In the free tier the form shows OmniSend branding/badge; remove it only by upgrading.
Trigger and frequency settings are the tutorial's preferences — test them against your own traffic.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Set up a welcome automation with a unique per-person discount code
cards.summary: Build an OmniSend welcome workflow triggered by the signup form that sends a sequence of emails containing a unique single-use discount code, and reuse that same code across the sequence.
cards.use_when: Retention: after a visitor subscribes, you want an automated welcome sequence that delivers a personal discount and nudges a first purchase.
steps: On the form, copy its name so you can match the form to the workflow.
In OmniSend Automation, choose a welcome workflow template (e.g. three-email version).
Set the trigger to 'subscribed via a signup form' and add a filter so only subscribers from this specific form (e.g. the 10% discount pop-up) enter — prevents cross-contamination between forms.
Adjust the wait nodes: remove or shorten the default wait if you want the first email to send immediately.

In the email, add a 'unique discount code' element; choose percent (e.g. 10%) or fixed amount, set the expiry (e.g. 7 days), and check 'reuse the unique discount code in this workflow' so the same code appears in later emails.
Personalise the subject line and body with a first-name variable, and note the discount expiry is calculated once and reused automatically — do not re-set it per email.
Style the email (rounded buttons, colors) to match the site, then finish editing and start the workflow to make it live.
Edit the follow-up emails (e.g. day 1 and day 4) to include the reused unique discount element and the same button.
caveats: The 10% discount, 7-day expiry and 1-day/4-day sends are the presenter's example values — pick numbers that protect your margin.
Workflows made with email-dependent code generation require the connected store; verify the discount element works before launching widely.
